name: Tayap

catalog_quote: Stressed syllables are realized as louder and longer than unstressed syllables. Stress in Tayap is generally not phonemic, and unpredictable stress occurs rarely. new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (realized as louder and longer) falls on the final syllable of an uninflected word, and inflected verbs are stressed on the final syllable of the whole word. Stress is a property of the lexical morpheme and stays put under affixation (munjé 'man' / munjénum 'men'; mɨrí 'forest' / mɨrínɨ 'in the forest'). Weight plays no role. Corroborated at p. 26 ('Stress is largely predictable, typically word final but occasionally occurring elsewhere in the word') and p. 342 ('the general rule that stress falls on the final syllable of a word').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. Reduplicated words retain stress on both halves (sumúsumú 'bat', towótowó 'four', p. 38), which is the only two-prominence pattern mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: About 2% of dictionary words carry unpredictable non-final stress, marked with an acute in the orthography (mbímaŋ 'leech', símbu 'maggot', arúmbatak 'fly', wákare 'no'); these are over three times as common with the vowel a. A few minimal pairs differ only by stress (tánkun 'I heard it' vs tankún 'I took it'). Peripheral case clitics and possessive clitics are unstressed. Verb exceptions conditioned by conjugation class and TAM: stress on the syllable preceding the perfect -(da)ra and intentional -(n)ana suffixes; on the counterfactual suffix -rɨk (vs the always-unstressed progressive -rɨk); on the final syllable of the verb stem in -ak progressives and in class-4 non-future verbs; on the ben object morpheme in transitive progressives; on the irrealis morpheme in intransitive irrealis duals; on the final syllable of the imperative stem rather than the word (mosé-tukun! 'buy it!'); subjunctive stems of class-4 verbs are always stressed.
new_statements.identity_note: The 2019 grammar describes the Tayap of Gapun village, Lower Sepik, PNG (the only community; spelled Taiap in Kulick's earlier work and in Glottolog). No dialect variation is at issue.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement between sources, not between the listed work and the catalog. The earlier sketch by the same first author, Kulick & Stroud 1992, 'The structure of the Taiap (Gapun) language', in Dutton, Ross & Tryon (eds), The Language Game (Pacific Linguistics C-110), p. 205 (already held by the project at, line 5958), says: 'Stress is predictable in Taiap. When a morpheme consists of two or three syllables, stress is generally placed on the second syllable. Stress placement in the verb is somewhat variable, depending on which suffixes are affixed to the verb stem.' For disyllables that coincides with the 2019 final rule, but for trisyllabic morphemes it predicts the penult where the 2019 grammar gives the final syllable with lexical exceptions (ambagái, makatók, toŋgodíp, minjiké vs. exceptional emári, atáwo). The 2019 grammar is the mature description (thirty years of fieldwork, a dictionary with stress marked on the ~2% exceptions) and explicitly states a word-final rule three times (pp. 26, 37, 342), so the 1992 second-syllable statement is treated as a superseded preliminary generalization, not as a competing analysis. The catalog's fixed: final syllable entry stands.

sources.quote: 'Stress is predictable in Taiap. When a morpheme consists of two or three syllables, stress is generally placed on the second syllable. Stress placement in the verb is somewhat variable, depending on which suffixes are affixed to the verb stem.' (Same page treats a-tukun 'eat' vs aa-tukun 'chop' as a vowel-LENGTH contrast, which the 2019 grammar p. 38 reanalyses as a STRESS minimal pair atukún vs átukun.)
sources.note: Only other Glottolog descriptive source; earlier preliminary analysis by the same first author says 'second syllable' of 2-3-syllable morphemes rather than 'final' -- agrees on predictable stress and on disyllables, diverges for trisyllables; superseded by the 2019 grammar (which lists trisyllabic final-stress forms ambagái, makatók, toŋgodíp and treats second-syllable trisyllables like atáwo, emári as lexical exceptions). Worth a one-line 'earlier analysis' note in the record, not a reclassify.
